title: Institutional reform: Outsider ideas need insider adoption
desc: Explains originality and uptake as complementary functions of outsider freedom and insider credibility, with background associations remaining non-deterministic.

kps.k: The cluster explains institutional change through the complementary roles of outsider originality and insider adoption.
kps.d: Both works link actors’ professional positions, networks and interests to the reforms they pursue. The Originality of Outsiders emphasises outsiders’ tendency to propose changes that displace existing arrangements; Insiders and Outsiders distinguishes generating ideas from securing their adoption and argues that sustained change often requires combining external perspectives with internal legitimacy. These are tendencies, not fixed actor categories or universal rules; sustaining versus disruptive and incremental versus radical describe spectra.

qs.q: This pattern ech- oes observations about innovation in other fields: insiders are more likely to propose  innovations with the intention of sustaining and updating existing practices, whereas  outsiders are more likely to develop innovations that may disrupt or displace existing  practices.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

qs.q: Separating out these two elements of the change process helps in explaining why outsiders typically have an advantage when it comes to originating innovations, particularly radical ones, whereas insiders frequently have an advantage when it comes to diffusion.
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Investment-treaty case studies associate officials’ backgrounds with reform proposals, rather than establishing that background determines reform.
kps.d: The Originality of Outsiders compares four cases: US and Bahraini officials rooted in arbitration proposed sustaining reforms, while EU and Brazilian officials without those roots proposed alternatives that would displace investor–state dispute settlement. The authors interpret this pattern through interdisciplinary innovation research and identify background as one factor shaping state proposals. The comparison concerns proposed reforms, not proof of their adoption or effectiveness; when individuals exert decisive influence, and how ministry dynamics shape their positions, remain unresolved.

qs.q: In the above four case studies, we see insider officials with deep roots in the arbitra- tion community propose sustaining innovations on behalf of the USA and Bahrain,  while outsider officials with no roots in the arbitration community propose disruptive  innovations that would displace ISDS on behalf of the EU and Brazil.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

qs.q: In identifying the backgrounds of officials as a factor that can shape the reform pro- posals put forward by their states, our work fits within a growing literature on the role  of individuals in shaping international law and institutions.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

kps.k: The proposed outsider advantage combines cognitive freedom, cross-field learning and weaker commitments to the status quo.
kps.d: Both works argue that outsiders can challenge entrenched assumptions, recombine ideas from different settings and pursue changes that threaten incumbents’ financial or reputational interests. They draw on psychology, sociology, research on outsider scientists and business illustrations; the shared General Motors example illustrates incumbent incentives rather than providing separate corroboration in each work. The Originality of Outsiders qualifies the cognitive argument with an inverted-U relationship between knowledge and creativity: unfamiliarity is not uniformly beneficial.

qs.q: Taking insiders and outsiders as ideal types, we suggest that outsiders often have an advantage when it comes to originating new innovations, particularly radical ones, on account of their diverse experiences and expertise, wide networks outside of the system, and lack of vested interest in the status quo.
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Originality does not ensure uptake: insider knowledge and credibility can determine whether proposals gain traction.
kps.d: Insiders and Outsiders argues that tacit knowledge, dense relationships, trust and continuity help insiders adapt proposals and sustain implementation. It cites a European environmental-NGO study in which farmers perceived organisations as outsiders and their proposals typically failed to gain traction. The Originality of Outsiders adds a tension rather than a direct disagreement: dismissal can obstruct diffusion but also allow disruptive ideas to develop before incumbents recognise the threat. Insider status itself does not guarantee long-term commitment.

qs.q: Here, insiders often have the advantage, on account of their specialized experiences and expertise, dense networks, high visibility, and credibility within the system, and staying power over time.
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Sometimes, insiders do not understand the threat posed by disruptive out- sider innovations until it is too late.27 For instance, successful camera companies like  Kodak failed to take low-quality cameras on mobile phones seriously until it was too  late and their business model was disrupted.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

kps.k: Hybrid actors and locally anchored coalitions offer practical ways to combine innovation with adoption.
kps.d: Insiders and Outsiders proposes insiders who retain external perspectives, outsiders who acquire internal advantages, and coalitions connecting both groups. Its Papua New Guinea SARV research illustrates exchanges of advocacy and legal knowledge, materials, funding connections, victim support and credibility. Observations suggest that insiders use resources more successfully when they request them than when outsiders impose them; local legitimacy and knowledge of needs remain a hypothesised explanation. Practical proposals include cross-sector taskforces, communities of practice and mixed-perspective groups, supported by repeated interaction, adequate resources and psychological safety.

qs.q: Although such hybrid individuals share many traits, it is helpful to distinguish between two categories of boundary-spanning actors: outsider–insiders, by which we mean insider individuals who have a special ability to see with outside eyes; and insider–outsiders, by which we mean outsider individuals who can skillfully draw on certain insider advantages.
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

qs.q: They included tangible resources, such as pamphlets and posters, as well as linking of the insider activist to funding networks or organizations that could assist in managing particular cases, such as providing ongoing support for any victims of SARV rescued by the insider activist.
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Cross-boundary collaboration can also cause alienation or capture, so capacity for change should not be confused with desirable change.
kps.d: The works largely complement rather than contradict each other. The central qualification comes from Insiders and Outsiders: hybrid actors may lose credibility, face accusations of betrayal or alienate both constituencies, drawbacks the authors also observe in their case study. Regulatory collaboration may require oversight and countervailing public-interest participation, not indiscriminate openness to industry influence. The framework claims to improve the likelihood of change, not guarantee success or establish its merits; why some boundary-spanning actors become effective catalysts remains open.

qs.q: Instead of bridging divides, they may fall between the cracks and, far from connecting everyone, they may end up alienating all sides.
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

qs.q: We see these drawbacks occurring in our own case study.
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition that outsider originality and insider adoption are complementary, while materially developing it into a broader framework for institutional change. Their common explanation is that outsiders may gain creative freedom from diverse experience, cross-field networks and weaker commitments to the status quo, whereas insiders contribute tacit knowledge, credibility, relationships and implementation capacity. Material internal variation concerns scope and prescription: The Originality of Outsiders chiefly offers a qualified association between officials’ backgrounds and the kinds of investment-treaty reforms they propose, without establishing determinism or fully specifying how adoption occurs. Insiders and Outsiders more directly extends the proposition by separating innovation from diffusion and proposing hybrid actors, locally anchored coalitions and cross-boundary networks to combine their advantages. It also adds practical conditions and risks, including adequate resources, psychological safety, loss of credibility, alienation and regulatory capture. These are tendencies and ideal types rather than universal categories, and the framework addresses capacity to produce change rather than whether any particular change is desirable. This characterisation applies only to the curated sources supplied, not academia or researchers generally.

qs.q: Separating out these two elements of the change process helps in explaining why outsiders typically have an advantage when it comes to originating innovations, particularly radical ones, whereas insiders frequently have an advantage when it comes to diffusion.
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

qs.q: The second strategy is based on networks, recognizing that links between insiders and outsiders may be particularly effective for enabling change (“inside–outside networked change”).
qs.a: Insiders and Outsiders: The Role of Human Agents and Networks in System Change · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source supports the principal proposition’s core distinction between outsider originality and insider-enabled uptake. Its investment-treaty case studies associate outsiders with more disruptive proposals and insiders with reforms that sustain existing arrangements, explaining the difference through professional experience, networks, cognitive freedom and vested interests. It also directly identifies outsiders’ lack of recognition as an obstacle to diffusion, consistent with the proposition that originality alone does not secure adoption. Material qualifications are that these are non-deterministic associations rather than universal rules, sustaining and disruptive innovation lie on a spectrum, and outsider dismissal can sometimes shelter an innovation until incumbents recognise its threat. The source does not develop the synthesis’s stronger practical prescription for insider–outsider coalitions or hybrid actors, so it supports rather than materially extends the proposition.

qs.q: This pattern ech- oes observations about innovation in other fields: insiders are more likely to propose  innovations with the intention of sustaining and updating existing practices, whereas  outsiders are more likely to develop innovations that may disrupt or displace existing  practices.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that outsider originality and insider adoption are complementary functions in institutional change. It explicitly separates innovation from diffusion: outsiders tend to benefit from broader perspectives, cross-system networks and weaker commitments to the status quo, while insiders tend to possess the tacit knowledge, relationships, credibility and continuity needed for ideas to gain traction. It also supports the proposition’s non-deterministic framing by treating insider and outsider positions as ideal types rather than fixed categories. The source adds practical detail—hybrid actors, insider–outsider coalitions, locally requested external resources, repeated interaction and psychological safety—but these mechanisms elaborate rather than materially redirect the proposition. Its qualifications do not amount to opposition: boundary-spanning actors may lose credibility, alienate both sides or enable capture, and combining outsider and insider strengths increases only the likelihood of change, not its success or desirability. Because this time period contains one curated source, these findings describe that source’s position and should not be read as evidence of wider prevalence.
